name: GPP (general physical preparedness)

image.caption: GPP = General Physical Preparedness. Also interpreted as, the freedom to eat and drink and walk to your heart's content and still keep on going.

lead: GPP, general physical preparedness, is the broad base of fitness an athlete builds before specialised training: strength, speed, endurance, flexibility and skill. People in physique-focused communities use it to raise their work capacity so they can handle more training and recover between sessions.

The appearance chain is indirect: better conditioning supports more and harder training, and more training supports muscle and leanness. Research on closely related high-intensity functional training describes gains in cardiorespiratory and strength measures.

paras: In practice GPP is done as sled pushes, carries, circuits, bodyweight work and easy aerobic work, often in the off-season or between heavy blocks, and is reduced when sport-specific work takes priority. Lifters include it to fill gaps in conditioning.

Injury risk depends on how hard and how varied the work is; reviews of high-intensity functional training in military settings discuss injury concerns and conclude that evidence to date does not clearly show higher rates than other programmes.

chain: Broad base of strength and conditioning
More productive training, supporting muscle and leanness
angle.text: GPP builds the base that lets people train more and recover between sessions, which supports muscle gain and body composition changes.

lead: General physical preparation (GPP) is the foundational phase of a training cycle that develops general strength, speed, endurance, flexibility, structure and skill before specific preparation (SPP) begins. It is emphasised in the off-season and kept lower during competition.[1]

In physique and strength communities, GPP is used to build work capacity, so athletes can do more volume and recover faster, which supports muscle gain and fat loss over time.[1] The phase can also help strengthen lagging muscles and support recovery from injuries.[1]
Research on related high-intensity functional training (HIFT) describes programmes designed to promote general physical preparedness through multi-joint functional movements.[2][3][4]
infobox: Strength, speed, endurance, flexibility, structure, skill[1]

paras: GPP opens each training cycle after restoration and uses general exercises and some specialised conditioning to work the major muscles and joints, preparing athletes for harder work such as explosive plyometrics.[1] In endurance sports GPP is described as 70 to 80 percent of training time, largely long slow distance.[1]

HIFT is defined as constantly varied functional, multi-joint movements and is distinct from high-intensity interval training.[2] A review in military medicine says HIFT workouts are designed to promote general physical preparedness, with debate over injury potential.[3] A companion paper argued concerns about injuries were not supported by the literature to date, while saying more research was needed.[4]
Studies of HIFT and military populations are reviewed above.[2][3][4] No studies found testing GPP as a distinct programme for appearance outcomes.
